extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, geometers, and advanced students interested in analytical geometry and nautical projection (Mercator) applications
extracted.subtask_description: Derivations and formulae for coordinate transformations between oblique axes, and a detailed study of the Mercator projection (projection of great circles and other spherical circles) including curvature, evolute, length, and classification of projected forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation between systems of oblique axes
rubrics_metrics.description: Let {µiµjµk}, {m'i m'j m'k} be the projecting coefficients of the new axes relative to the old, and {rni rnj rnk}, {r'i r'j r'k} those of the old axes relative to the new. If (x,y,z) and (x',y',z') denote the same point the projecting-coefficient equations (93),(94) give x = f11 x' + f12 y' + f13 z', y = f21 x' + f22 y' + f23 z', z = f31 x' + f32 y' + f33 z', and their inverses; these equations enable the required transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page shows how to form the projecting-coefficient relations (eqs. (93),(94)), eliminate variables to express new coordinates in terms of old (and vice versa), and compute all projecting coefficients f_ij by using relations analogous to Lagrange's relations among directing cosines. See also formulas (96) giving explicit determinant-like expressions for the f_ij in terms of the m', n', r' etc., and subsequent simplifications when axes are rectangular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant / volume relation for coordinate transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Equating the volume of the tetrahedron formed by unit distances on the old axes expressed in the new axes leads to the relation (95): an alternating-sum expression in the projecting coefficients equals ±1/F (or ±4 V etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the origin measure on the axes OL, OM, ON each equal to unity; the volume V of the tetrahedron expressed via the projecting coefficients yields v = ± 1/4 [r' f' i^wV' — rww ...] and equating with the volume computed as 1/6 OL·OM·ON leads to equation (95). This determinant-like relation is used to relate the two systems' cubature coefficients and to compute projecting coefficients (see surrounding discussion and (95)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations among projecting coefficients and directing cosines (orthogonality relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are multiple supplementary relations among the projecting coefficients and directing cosines, e.g. equations (99)-(103) and (101)-(104) giving orthogonality and normalization constraints; special simplifications occur when one or both systems are rectangular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare values obtained from substituting transformations into each other (see (99),(100),(101),(102),(103)). These give equalities like sums of products of coefficients equalling 0 or 1, analogous to orthogonality and normalization of direction cosines. The text explains how these relations reduce in the rectangular-axis cases (F=1 or F'=1) and how to compute unknowns accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation when new coordinate planes are given (plane-to-plane formulas)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the equations of the new coordinate planes y'z', z'x', x'y' are A1 x + B1 y + C1 z = D1, A2 x + B2 y + C2 z = D2, A3 x + B3 y + C3 z = D3 (eqs. (115)-(117)), then the projecting coefficients and directing cosines of the new axes are deduced from these plane coefficients and the new origin, and the new coordinates are given by explicit formulas (see (118)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page derives the projecting coefficients of each new axis from the plane equations (using minors and combinations of A_i, B_i, C_i), computes directing cosines of plane normals, forms P (a polynomial combination of plane coefficients) and uses these to write the new coordinates as rational expressions in the old coordinates (eqs. (115)-(118)). The method yields both new-in-terms-of-old and inverse relations by solving the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental differential relation for Mercator projection (meridional parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinitesimal correspondence between sphere and Mercator chart: dφ/dY = 1 / cos Y = sec Y (noting φ denotes the chart meridional measure corresponding to true latitude Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From similarity of infinitesimal elements the text derives df/dY = 1/cos Y (equation (1) in the Mercator section). Integrating these meridional parts (sum of secants) gives the meridional-part tables used in nautical practice. This differential relation is the starting point for the integration producing the standard Mercator formula (see next entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercator projection formula for projected latitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrated formula: y = log_e cot (45° − Y/2) (equation (2)), or in common logs with the appropriate multiplicative constant for nautical miles: y (nautical miles) = 7915.705 log_10 cot(comp. of lat.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page shows the substitution z = sin Y, integrates the secant-series to obtain y = log cot(45° − Y/2) (equation (2)). It also gives practical conversion to nautical miles by multiplying common logarithm by 7915.705 and demonstrates a worked example for latitude 37°48'. The formula is central to computing projected meridional parts on the chart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation and comparison with cylindrical (enveloping cylinder) projection
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison: in the simple enveloping-cylinder projection the true latitude Y is represented by its tangent, tan Y = Y' (if Y' is the projected latitude), while in Mercator projection the relation between tan Y and the Mercator meridional measure y can be expressed by derived relations (text derives links between tan Y, tan Y', and y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article derives relations connecting tan Y and y (and shows how the two projections compare numerically for given angles). It shows, for example, that for certain numeric values the projected latitudes under the two schemes differ (examples given: y = 1 corresponds to Y = 49°36'18" for Mercator vs Y' = 46° for the cylindrical case). Use the derivations in the text to convert between representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projected great circle curve: elliptic-function representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The projection of a great circle onto a Mercator chart has simple arcs which are represented by an elliptic function of the first order; equations (3) and (8) (and subsequent derivations) give relations tan Y = sin x · tan A and differential/arc-length formulae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a great circle with maximum latitude A, coordinates on the chart (x,y) satisfy tan Y = sin x · tan A (eq. (3)), and y = M log cot(45° − Y/2) (eq. (2)), which together give the parametric form for the projected curve. The text proceeds to compute radius of curvature, evolute, and to show arc-length elements are expressible by elliptic functions of the first order (see derivation around eq. (8) and surrounding paragraphs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Radius of curvature and evolute coordinates for projected circles
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas for radius of curvature r and coordinates (a, β) of the evolute are given in closed form for the projected curves. For example, at the vertex r = cosec A; more general expressions like r^ = cosec^ Y + cot^ x − cot' Y + cosec^ a (and other simpler forms in special cases) are derived, and evolute coordinates a = x − tan x·? and β = y − sin x·cosec^ P (various specific forms appear in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manuscript computes curvature via differential relations between sphere and chart: ds/dx etc., uses spherical triangles to express cotangents and sine relations, and derives expressions for r and for the coordinates of the center of curvature (evolute) in terms of x, y, Y, A, P. These are accompanied by geometric interpretation (vertex, asymptotes) and numeric tables for examples (see sections on evolute and radius of curvature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of projected curve expressed via elliptic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of arc on the chart relates to the spherical element by ds/dz etc., and the resulting expression for arc-length of projected great-circle arcs is representable by an elliptic function of the first order (see eq. (8) and subsequent integration leading to elliptic integrals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differential relations derived (e.g. ds/dx = 1/(1 − sin^2 A cos^2 x)^{1/2} times a factor) lead to integral expressions for lengths. The text shows how to multiply through and set constants to write arcs in terms of elliptic functions; see the derivation that follows eq. (8) for the full development and the remark that no additional constant is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of projected circles on Mercator chart (three canonical forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: All circles of the sphere fall into three classes regarding their Mercator projection: (1) circumferences not including a pole produce symmetric wavering forms similar to projected great circles; (2) circumferences passing through a pole produce curves of two infinite branches (vertex on a parallel; meridians 90° from the vertex are asymptotes); (3) circumferences including a pole produce elliptical forms (finite symmetric figure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives geometric construction and equations for each class, shows how the three forms are related in limiting cases (circles through pole are limits of the others), and supplies formulas for maxima/minima, asymptotes, and how to place the parallel-of-symmetry. See the section enumerating the three classes and the detailed derivations that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projected circle extremal longitude and related latitude formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: For circles not including a pole, there is a maximum longitude X (east and west of the meridian of the vertex) where the meridians touch the circle; sin X (or sin of that longitude) and the latitude of touching points obey relations derived from right-angled spherical triangles: e.g. sin CPE = sin EC = sin/?P · sin?p (text gives the spherical-triangle relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manuscript derives expressions for the extremal longitude X, the corresponding latitudes, and integrates to find chart y-values producing expressions like y = log (sec Zi + tan Zi) or y = ± log cot(45° − x/2) depending on sign conventions. Use these relations when locating projected extremes and computing chart coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for equal tangents from a point to the parabola y^2 = 4 m x
rubrics_metrics.description: To find when the two tangents from point (a, β) to parabola y^2 = 4 m x are equal, form the chord of contact (equation (1)), write the perpendicular from (a, β) to that line, eliminate y and obtain an abscissa x; the condition that the two tangents be equal reduces to an algebraic condition leading to either β = 0 (the axis) or the locus equation (the text: "This equation is satisfied either by /3 = 0, or 0^ ^ 4sw").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives the chord-of-contact equation and the perpendicular construction leading to eliminations and root relations (see eqs. (1)-(5)). It concludes that equal tangents can only be drawn from a point on the principal axis (β = 0) unless the point lies on the locus given by the coalescence condition (the locus where the two tangents coalesce in a single contact point). The full algebraic derivation is presented step-by-step in the text.
